title: SCLS: Shapelet-based soft contrastive learning for multivariate time series clustering
abstract: Multivariate time series clustering aims to group sequences into coherent patterns, playing a vital role in time series analysis. While shapelets-based methods combined with contrastive learning have shown potential, they often depend on data augmentation, which introduces noise and uncertainty, and the extracted shapelets may deviate from true subsequences, limiting interpretability and clustering quality. To address these challenges, we propose a shapelets-based soft contrastive learning method for multivariate time series clustering, called SCLS, to improve clustering performance. The method consists of four stages. First, an attention mechanism is used to fuse multiple feature components from the original sequence, which helps to reduce uncertainty and extract more representative shapelets. Second, a perceptually important points selection method based on information gain is applied to mine multi-scale shapelets. Third, a shapelet encoder enhanced with a pseudo-label clustering mechanism is developed to embed shapelets into structure-aware representations for subsequent learning. Finally, a hierarchical soft contrastive learning strategy is introduced to jointly optimize the shapelets representation space at both the temporal level and the sample level, producing representations that are more suitable for clustering analysis. We conducted extensive experiments on dozens of real-world datasets to evaluate the clustering quality. The results show that SCLS achieves the highest performance ranking compared with state-of-the-art methods.

title: A comprehensive online active ensemble learning framework for multi-class imbalanced data streams with concept drift
abstract: Many real-world streaming applications face the simultaneous challenges of multi-class imbalance, concept drift, and limited labeling resources. Existing methods usually address only part of this setting, such as binary imbalance, fully supervised data streams, or relatively stable class-prior distributions. However, in practical online environments, class priors and decision boundaries may evolve together, and the majority or minority role of a class may change over time. To address this problem, this paper proposes CADEE, a comprehensive online active ensemble learning framework for multi-class imbalanced data streams with concept drift. CADEE integrates an online ensemble classifier, an ADWIN-based drift detector, a prediction register, an incremental trainer, a label sliding window, and a sample sliding window into a unified online learning loop. First, a class-aware dynamic performance calibration mechanism is designed to evaluate base classifiers using class-level performance, uncertainty, confidence, and complementary diversity, thereby reducing majority class dominance in ensemble fusion. Second, a drift-adaptive ensemble size and multi-dimensional diversity regulation mechanism is introduced to adjust ensemble capacity according to drift severity and member complementarity, improving adaptability during abrupt changes while avoiding unnecessary expansion in stable periods. Third, a multi-factor adaptive hard-example sampling and mixing enhancement strategy is developed to select informative boundary and minority-related samples under limited label budgets and to generate quality-controlled same-class Mixup samples for incremental training. Experiments on 15 synthetic multi-class imbalanced data streams with different drift patterns and 5 real-world data streams show that CADEE achieves competitive or superior performance compared with several state-of-the-art methods in terms of Accuracy, Kappa, G-Mean, Recall, and average ranking. The results demonstrate that CADEE can improve label utilization, drift adaptation, and minority class recognition in non-stationary multi-class imbalanced data streams.

title: Automated fault detection and predictive quality control in software system using advanced deep learning techniques
abstract: Software fault prediction is a crucial application of machine learning that focuses on identifying fault-prone components in software systems before they cause failures. It helps improve software reliability, optimize testing efforts, and reduce maintenance costs by analyzing historical data and code metrics. However, challenges such as poor data quality, class imbalance, and limited model generalizability can hinder the accuracy and effectiveness of predictions. In this manuscript, automated fault detection and predictive quality control in software system using advanced deep learning techniques are proposed. The goal is to accurately and adaptively predict software faults, enabling timely detection of defect-prone modules and improving software quality and maintenance efficiency. First, the software defect prediction dataset is used to collect input data. Fuzzy consensus cubature information filtering (FCCIF) is then used to preprocess the data in order to remove noise, clean it up, and normalize it. The feature selection procedure then uses the preprocessed data using superb fairy-wren optimization algorithm (SFOA) select the relevant features. Then, the relevant features fed into the prediction and classification using spatio-temporal Aatention-based hidden physics-informed neural network (STAHPINN) is used to predict the software fault prediction and classification such as non-defect and defect. The weight parameters of STAHPINN are then optimized using the enzyme action optimizer (EAO). When compared to other existing techniques such artificial neural networks, YOLOv5, and deep learning, the suggested Python-based method shows notable gains in accuracy, precision, f1-score, recall, and Matthews correlation coefficient. The proposed method achieve 99.3% accuracy, 0.002% MAE error, and the 0.8Sec computational time, the proposed method result values is better than other exiting methods.

title: Differentiable evidence selection with credibility-aware multi-document reasoning for fake news detection
abstract: Existing graph-based evidence-aware fake news detection methods preserve structured claim–evidence semantics, but evidence filtering is often detached from downstream reasoning, and candidate documents are commonly aggregated independently. To address these limitations, we propose DES-CMR , whose central mechanism is selection-guided multi-document reasoning. The model first learns a claim-conditioned sparse evidence distribution \(\varvec{\omega }\) in an end-to-end manner. Rather than serving only as a preliminary filtering score, \(\varvec{\omega }\) is injected as a prior into inter-evidence attention and is reused during final evidence aggregation. After cross-document interaction refines the candidate representations, a distinct post-reasoning distribution \(\varvec{\pi }\) is recomputed, allowing the model to preserve or revise the initial evidence selection according to complementary, redundant, and conflicting relations. Task-learned source embeddings and a bounded source-conditioned logit residual supplement textual relevance, while validation-aware decision-boundary selection stabilizes probability-to-label conversion. Prompt-guided graph encoding and adversarial supervised contrastive learning provide the representation and optimization backbone. Experiments on Snopes and PolitiFact show that DES-CMR consistently outperforms representative pattern-based, evidence-based, and graph-based baselines. Component, robustness, decision-boundary, complexity, and sensitivity analyses further examine the effectiveness and limitations of the proposed reasoning mechanism.

title: Dnmma: dual-modality noise mitigation and multi-granularity augmentation for multimodal relation extraction in social media
abstract: Multimodal Relation Extraction (MRE) is a pivotal process in information retrieval and knowledge graph construction. Nevertheless, its performance is often constrained by the inherently low quality of social media data. Prior studies have largely focused on alleviating visual noise, while two critical issues remain underexplored: (1) unreliable of semantic extraction caused by intrinsic textual noise in short, informal posts, and (2) insufficient fine-grained alignment, where coarse-grained visual features often introduce irrelevant interference rather than effective relational evidence. To address these issues, we propose DNMMA, a Dual-Modality Noise Mitigation and Multi-Granularity Augmentation framework for social media MRE. Central to DNMMA is a Textual Token Refinement network that distills concise semantic representations from noisy inputs, establishing a reliable foundation for knowledge representation. To maximize the utility of the visual modality, we develop a multi-granularity visual augmentation strategy that incorporates hierarchical fusion, global features, and local regions. Specifically, an Adaptive Semantic Mixup balances visual diversity and text-image consistency by adaptively fusing synthetic and original images. Furthermore, a Role-Aware Attention mechanism explicitly incorporates textual entity roles to suppress noisy visual features, while Salient Visual Augmentation strengthens the discriminative power of local key regions. After refining both modalities, DNMMA performs joint entity relation optimization for relation extraction. Extensive experiments on the MNRE and MRE-MI datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DNMMA in social media multimodal relation extraction.

title: A multi-view graph learning approach with RoBERTa for Twitter sentiment analysis
abstract: Sentiment analysis on Twitter is difficult because tweets are short, informal, and context‑dependent. To tackle these challenges, we propose a hybrid model that combines contextual language modeling with graph‑based structural learning. Each tweet is first split into sentences and smaller semantic chunks to capture multiple levels of structure. The text is then encoded with a pretrained RoBERTa model, producing contextual embeddings that represent the meaning of each token. Using these embeddings, we build two complementary graphs. The first is a sentence‑level graph, where each node represents a sentence. A Graph Attention Network (GATv2) is applied to learn how strongly each sentence contributes to the overall sentiment. The second is a chunk‑level graph that models local relationships between neighboring text segments. A graph isomorphism network (GIN) aggregates these local features and captures distributed sentiment cues. Finally, the global representation from RoBERTa, the sentence‑level features from GAT, and the chunk‑level features from GIN are combined through an adaptive fusion layer and passed to a classifier. Experiments on the Twitter US Airline and Sentiment140 benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed par-ser-free multi-view framework. The proposed model consistently outperforms strong baseline methods, while comprehensive experiments confirm the complementary contributions of the sentence-level graph, chunk-level graph, and adaptive fusion module. The source code for reproducing our results can be found at ( https://github.com/hashemparvin/Sentiment-Analysis.git ).

title: Information-theoretic drift detection using KL divergence and tolerance time in Sliding Adaptive Beta Distribution Models
abstract: Concept drift detection is a critical challenge in dynamic data stream environments, where changes in data distribution can compromise model accuracy over time. This study presents an enhanced drift detection framework, which integrates Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence and tolerance time into Sliding Adaptive Beta Distribution Models (SABeDM). The incorporation of KL divergence enables precise quantification of distributional shifts between consecutive data windows, improving sensitivity to both abrupt and subtle drifts. Simultaneously, the concept of tolerance time introduces temporal flexibility, allowing the model to accommodate minor delays or fluctuations without triggering false alarms. Experimental evaluations across six benchmark datasets (SEA_a, SEA_g, MIXD, HYP, PHI, and WET) demonstrate consistent and superior performance over state-of-the-art methods including SRP, ADWIN, DDM, and EDDM. For instance, on the SEA_a dataset, \({\text{S}\text{A}\text{B}\text{e}\text{D}\text{M}}^{kl}\) achieves an accuracy of 83.50% and F1-score of 82.75%, compared to 73.68% and 73.87% by SRP. On the complex PHI dataset, it reaches 96.10% accuracy and 96.15% F1-score, outperforming all baselines. Similar improvements are observed across precision, recall, and other datasets, with notable robustness on real-world data such as WET, where \({\text{S}\text{A}\text{B}\text{e}\text{D}\text{M}}^{kl}\) boosts the F1-score to 69.00% from 60.19% (SRP). The proposed approach exhibits superior adaptability, minimal detection latency, and robust performance in high-dimensional and complex data settings. These findings highlight the efficacy of information-theoretic integration for real-time, accurate, and resilient concept drift detection in evolving data streams.

title: Advancing object-centric process mining with multi-dimensional data operations
abstract: Abstract Analyzing process data at varying levels of granularity is important to derive actionable insights and support informed decision-making. Object-Centric Event Data (OCED) enhance process mining by capturing interactions among events and multiple objects, leading to the discovery of more detailed and realistic yet complex process models. The lack of methods to adjust the granularity of the analysis prevents users from leveraging the full potential of Object-Centric Process Mining (OCPM). To address this gap, we propose four operations: drill-down, roll-up, unfold, and fold, which enable analysts to change the granularity of analysis when working with Object-Centric Event Logs (OCEL). These operations allow analysts to seamlessly transition between detailed and aggregated process models, facilitating the discovery of insights that require varying levels of abstraction. We formally define these operations and implement them in an open-source Python library. To validate their utility, we applied the approach to real-world OCEL data extracted from a learning management system, covering a four-year period and approximately 400 students, as a case of object-centric educational process mining. This case study shows significant improvements in the precision and fitness of the discovered models after applying the operations. In addition, we evaluate the scalability of the operators on large, publicly available OCELs derived from the Business Process Intelligence Challenge datasets, demonstrating that the operations remain computationally feasible on industrial-scale event logs. This approach can empower analysts to perform more flexible and comprehensive process exploration, unlocking actionable insights through flexible granularity adjustments.

title: Dynamic stream clustering for real-time schema profiling with DSC+
abstract: Abstract Streaming applications often involve several sources that continuously produce data in diverse formats—for instance, IoT applications may receive heterogeneous messages from different devices. In such a scenario, technicians are interested in characterizing the incoming traffic to understand which kinds of data are flowing into the stream; this activity is called schema profiling and consists of producing key insights about the schema of data in a high-variety context. In this paper, we present a streaming approach to schema profiling called DSC+ (Dynamic Stream Clustering). The approach works under the overlapping sliding window paradigm and produces profiles by clustering the schemas extracted from the data according to the k-means algorithm. DSC+ is a two-phase algorithm: schemas are pre-aggregated into a coreset using a compact data structure called schema features and then clustered. Unlike previous approaches, DSC+ is designed to work in a dynamic and unknown domain, where the number of schema attributes is variable and is not known a priori. DSC+ implements rules to dynamically and efficiently update the profile in real-time, minimizing the computations at every slide of the window while maintaining consistency with the principles of k-means. Experiments are carried out on both real and synthetic datasets to demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposal against related state-of-the-art algorithms.

title: Contrastive hallucination impact mitigation and evaluation for zero-shot dense retrieval systems
abstract: Zero-shot dense retrieval enables search systems to be deployed in new domains without task-specific relevance labels by mapping queries and documents into a shared semantic space. Classical dense retrievers often struggle with query-document asymmetry, especially in engineering applications such as enterprise knowledge bases and educational question-answering platforms. Hypothetical Document Embeddings (HyDE) use large language models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-documents aligning queries with relevant documents, but these often contain hallucinations that degrade retrieval quality. We present CHIME (Contrastive Hallucination Impact Mitigation and Evaluation), a hallucination-aware framework for zero-shot dense retrieval. CHIME mitigates hallucinations via contrastive fine-tuning with hybrid negative sampling to separate query-relevant content from confounding hallucinations—without target-domain relevance labels. For evaluation, CHIME introduces Hallucination Impact Assessment (HIA), combining a clause-level Hallucination Severity Score (HSS) with a Retrieval Degradation Index (RDI) quantifying hallucination impact on nDCG@10 relative to a non-generated baseline. Experiments on eight BEIR datasets show that CHIME improves retrieval effectiveness on the majority of tasks, with an average gain of 6.5% nDCG@10 and up to 13.5% on fine-grained tasks. Analysis further reveals that reducing hallucination severity alone does not guarantee better retrieval; RDI correlates much more strongly with nDCG@10 improvements than HSS, indicating that which hallucinations are removed matters more than how many. CHIME requires no target-domain relevance labels, is resource-efficient, and is readily deployable in real-world retrieval systems under label scarcity and safety constraints. Our code is available at https://github.com/SleepyLH/CHIME .

title: A topic semantic relational knowledge-enhanced conversational model for improving response accuracy
abstract: In multi-turn conversations, insufficient knowledge reasoning and ambiguity caused by missing entities often hinder the system’s ability to effectively leverage conversation history, resulting in inaccurate responses. To address this issue, this paper proposes a Topic Semantic Relational Knowledge (TSR) model that integrates external knowledge to resolve ambiguity and enhance dialogue comprehension. The TSR model first retrieves historical dialogue utterances based on the semantics of the current conversation, filters them to extract topic-relevant history utterances, and combines them with the current dialogue to form topic semantic information. This information is subsequently used for semantic matching with external knowledge to strengthen reasoning. Additionally, a Global Knowledge Attention Layer (GKA) is introduced to fully exploit knowledge by capturing richer knowledge representations through multilayer feature fusion. Experiments conducted on the QuAC, CoQA, and DoQA datasets demonstrate that the TSR model achieves state-of-the-art performance in both F1 and Human Equivalence Score at the Dialog level (HEQ-D) metrics. The TSR model shows significant improvements in handling multi-turn conversations, leading to more accurate and contextually relevant responses.

title: Discovering session-level demand patterns for reinforcement learning-based dynamic inventory allocation in live-streaming e-commerce
abstract: Live-streaming e-commerce is rapidly reshaping retail supply chains, creating an environment where traditional inventory planning methods fall short. The primary challenge is the high-stakes nature of pre-session inventory allocation; misjudging the demand for a single, hours-long event can lead to significant lost sales from stockouts or capital waste from overstocking. Historical forecasting is often unreliable as the demand is heavily influenced by session-specific factors, including the session hosts, the product assortment, and expected user engagement. This study develops an integrated framework that begins with session-based demand forecasting, utilizing a rich blend of historical data and engagement-proxy features to accurately predict total demand for products within a given live-streaming event. Building on this framework, we propose a dynamic inventory orchestration mechanism. This mechanism uses session-specific forecasting to automate and optimize the crucial pre-session task of allocating inventory from a central supply to the live-streaming event, ensuring the right amount of stock is in the right place at the right time. The model’s core forecasting engine was empirically validated on a synthetic dataset of 500 live-streaming sessions derived from public Taobao and Twitch sources. The arithmetic-mean ensemble of 10 independently trained Gradient Boosting Machines achieved the highest accuracy, with a mean R-squared of 0.9364 and the lowest standard deviation across 20 independent runs. Furthermore, we enhance the inventory orchestration stage with a tabular Q-learning agent that learns optimal ordering policies directly from demand sequences, converging within approximately 900 episodes and achieving a 93.3% fill rate while dynamically balancing holding, stockout, and ordering costs. The methodological contribution is an integrated, session-aware framework that couples ensemble forecasting with reinforcement learning-driven orchestration in a live-streaming-specific supply chain context. This research contributes a practical, data-driven solution that enhances supply chain agility by enabling dynamic, intelligent, and automated inventory decisions in the fast-paced world of live-streaming e-commerce sessions.

title: High utility itemsets mining in data stream using cuckoo search
abstract: Traditional deterministic algorithms for mining high utility itemsets in data streams often run into memory explosion problems and can easily run out of memory with large, dense datasets. Most current metaheuristic methods just adapt generic swarm-intelligence frameworks and miss out on customized mechanisms for sliding window data stream scenarios, which can lead to itemset loss, slow convergence, and lots of redundant fitness evaluations from duplicate candidate itemsets. So, this paper picks cuckoo search as the base metaheuristic population search framework and develops three sets of cooperative specialized strategies for mining high utility itemsets in data streams, leading to the SHUIM-CS algorithm. First, for the non-differentiable nature of the binary discrete itemset search space, a discrete pseudo-gradient position update strategy based on utility differences is designed, with bit flipping used to evolve individuals, cutting down itemset loss in metaheuristic algorithms and speeding up population convergence. Next, a BARS block-based circular buffer index structure is built, integrated with the SWIA sliding window incremental index tree, using arrays to circularly store transaction blocks and update window utility incrementally at a logarithmic scale, easing memory bottlenecks in large, dense data streams. Finally, an HRM result mapping strategy using double-hash probing is proposed to remove duplicate candidate itemsets and cut out redundant fitness calculations. Experiments on multiple real and synthetic datasets compare metaheuristic and deterministic baselines, and ablation experiments verify the effectiveness of the three core strategies. Plus, theoretical analyses on pruning safety, hash mechanism performance, and algorithm complexity are included. The results show SHUIM-CS has clear memory advantages and is way more suitable for large-scale data stream mining when memory is limited.

title: Sparcent: faster multi-vector dense retrieval with sparse centroid indices
abstract: Multi-vector dense retrieval methods have set the state-of-the-art retrieval quality on ranking tasks. However, the superior effectiveness of such methods comes with substantial computational overhead, which makes their deployment in large-scale search engines infeasible. As a remedy, we propose a novel approach, Sparcent , that leverages learned sparse retrieval (LSR) to accelerate the query-centroid matching stage in multi-vector dense retrieval. Specifically, we first derive sparse centroid representations for multi-vector term-embedding clusters and then prune them, producing compact centroid vectors that remain both efficient and effective for the indexing via LSR methods. Next, we integrate Sparcent with two well-known multi-vector retrieval systems, PLAID and WARP , already optimized for single-core CPU search. Our experimental results show that Sparcent provides up to 4.6 \(\times \) speed-up over the original PLAID and 1.3 \(\times \) speed-up over WARP , respectively, with virtually zero additional memory, while maintaining result effectiveness on both in-domain and out-of-domain retrieval tasks.

title: Entity resolution across SQL and NoSQL database management systems: a comprehensive review
abstract: In the era where data are often referred to as the new oil, entity resolution (ER) plays a pivotal role in identifying and linking records that represent the same real-world entity across disparate sources. While existing surveys emphasize algorithmic advancements, they largely overlook how database architectures fundamentally shape ER technique selection and performance. This paper presents a comprehensive, database-centric review of ER techniques across SQL and NoSQL Database Management Systems. We systematically classify ER techniques using a three-dimensional framework encompassing data model characteristics, system architecture, and target workloads. Through structured taxonomies, we demonstrate how ER techniques—from traditional rule-based methods to advanced deep learning methods—adapt their implementation and optimization strategies across different paradigms. The review culminates in actionable guidelines that enable practitioners to select appropriate ER techniques aligned with their specific data infrastructure, bridging the gap between algorithmic innovation and practical, database-aware deployment.

title: Explainable risk prediction and prescriptive decision support with deterministic RAG in industrial textile manufacturing
abstract: Industrial textile manufacturing requires decision support systems that not only estimate quality-related risk but also translate model outputs into interpretable and operationally meaningful decision support information. This study proposes a leakage-aware and artifact-grounded framework for explainable risk prediction and model-consistent decision support in textile production. A transparent 0–100 CompositeRiskScore is defined as a retrospective quality risk proxy based on quality, meter difference, downtime, and production duration components. For prediction, only pre-QC production, planning, and process descriptors are used as input variables. The proposed framework integrates local explanations, Soft Direction-Consistency filtering, train-only low-risk reference bands, model-consistent what-if checks, and a locked context retrieval interface over structured JSON artifacts into a unified decision support workflow. Rather than treating model attributions as direct prescriptions, the explanation layer organizes them into recommendation candidates with explicit actionability levels, including real-time adjustable, setup-level adjustable, planning/procurement-level adjustable, and contextual feature groups. Candidate changes are evaluated using model-consistent what-if checks that measure whether the proposed changes reduce the model-predicted CompositeRiskScore . These checks quantify internal trained model response and are not evidence that applying the changes will improve realized production quality. The main evaluation uses a roll-group-disjoint split to prevent analytical rows linked to the same roll-level production group from crossing the Train, Validation, and Test partitions. Under this evaluation setting, the model achieves more moderate but meaningful risk-ranking performance, while unseen pattern and unseen loom scenarios remain more challenging generalization settings. The retrieval layer is designed as a structured decision support interface rather than an open-ended RAG reasoning system. It uses a single primary context, preserves locked prediction and explanation fields, excludes post-QC and ground-truth information from deployment-facing answers, and returns an explicit “not available in context” fallback when requested information is absent from the selected context. The results show that the proposed framework can transform leakage-controlled risk predictions into traceable explanation, recommendation, and retrieval artifacts.

title: $$\Delta $$Semantics: a neuro-symbolic framework for dynamic ontological reasoning with proof-carrying machine learning
abstract: This study presents \(\Delta \) Semantics, a unified neuro-symbolic framework for reasoning with versioned ontologies, checker-validated proof certificates, and calibrated set-valued outputs. The framework maintains a typed ontology \(\Delta _t\) , synthesizes candidate rules through Path-to-Rule and Prompt-to-Rule , and applies propose–verify–repair inference across HotpotQA, FB15k-237, and Visual Genome. On FB15k-237, Hits@10 remains \(0.1400\) across the pre-adaptation ontology versions on \(n=20{,}466\) test queries, whereas MRR decreases from \(0.1064\) to \(0.0921\) after 10,000 entailed edges are enabled at \(\Delta _2\) . A brief post-update adaptation step raises MRR to \(0.1013\) , recovering \(64.3\%\) of the initial loss, while Hits@1 increases from \(0.0650\) to \(0.0739\) , Hits@3 from \(0.0980\) to \(0.1070\) , and Hits@10 from \(0.1400\) to \(0.1404\) . Proof pass also increases from \(95.6\) to \(97.1\%\) , and the ontology-violation rate decreases from \(0.11\) to \(0.03\%\) . The TransE, ComplEx, and RotatE results serve only as protocol-matched reference points; the central contribution concerns proof-carrying inference and controlled adaptation to ontology updates rather than leaderboard-oriented knowledge-graph completion. On HotpotQA, EM increases modestly from \(58.6\) to \(59.8\) , while mapped support reaches \(0.8274\) and \(92.6\%\) of accepted predictions receive checker-validated proof certificates. On Visual Genome, mR@50 increases from \(6.8\) to \(8.9\) , mR@100 from \(7.9\) to \(10.2\) , and type compliance from \(82.4\) to \(96.7\%\) , with a proof-pass rate of \(94.6\%\) . These results support a unified implementation for auditable reasoning under ontology change and show that post-update adaptation can recover much, but not all, of the rank degradation caused by a logical update.

title: Enhancing fault prediction in SOA-based systems via hybrid transformer–BiLSTM with COA–SCSO feature selection method
abstract: In today’s dynamic software ecosystems, ensuring the reliability of service-oriented architecture (SOA)-based systems has become increasingly critical. As these systems scale, their complexity introduces challenges in fault detection, often leading to service disruptions that are costly and difficult to diagnose. Making sure SOA-based systems reliability is becoming more and more important. To the best of our knowledge, fault prediction is still challenging in SOA environments due to high dimensionality, temporal dependencies, and class imbalance in service data. Models for predicting fault-prone modules most often use simple classifiers, or rely on static features without considering these complex aspects. To overcome this issue, we proposed a new hybrid framework that combines the Transformer Encoder and a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network. The global dependency is captured by self-attention and for the temporal patterns (bidirectional) a BiLSTM that would compose the new architecture applied to SOA fault prediction. We propose a dual-strategy-based feature selection and optimization method to achieve even better performance. This method takes advantage of both the exploratory characteristics of Coati optimization algorithm (COA) and the exploitative behavior of the sand cat swarm optimization (SCSO). This hybridization combines exploration and exploitation for the first time in software fault prediction to reduce the redundancy, address imbalanced data, and choose the most informative service features. The proposed method achieves better performance than state-of-the-art methods. We achieved accuracy of 99.0%, precision of 98.2%, recall of 98.5%, F1-score of 98.3%, ROC-AUC of 99.2%, and an MCC value of 97.1% respectively. The performance improvement of the proposed method is up to 4.5% in accuracy, 5.1% in precision, 3.7% in recall, 4.4% in F1-score, 2% in ROC-AUC, and 8.2% in MCC. These results support a strong quantitative indication of its effectiveness and robustness. The statistical validation demonstrates that the observed performance improvements are consistent across the evaluated cross-validation folds. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for SOA fault prediction under the evaluated benchmark setting. Further validation is required to assess its robustness under heterogeneous and dynamically evolving service environments.

title: Cluster-based domain adaptation: toward fine-grained similarity-aware graph transfer learning
abstract: Graph transfer learning has emerged as a powerful approach for leveraging knowledge from source domains to enhance model performance in target domains. Recently, unsupervised graph domain adaptation (UGDA), as a transfer learning method that transfers knowledge requiring no labeled data in the target domain, is attracting increasing attention. However, existing UGDA methods treat each domain as a single unified entity, which overlooks the fine-grained similarity across domains. Fine-grained similarity refers to the phenomenon where data in the source domain exhibit stronger relevance to specific parts of data in the target domain. Ignoring fine-grained similarity introduces interactions between less relevant data, hence hindering UGDA models from achieving better performance. To address this challenge, we propose cluster-based domain adaptation (CDA). CDA introduces fine-grained similarity-aware domain adaptation to promote semantically relevant interactions between source and target domain. Specifically, to adapt to the cross-domain clustering scenario, we design a domain-aware clustering approach that mitigates the imbalance between source and target data during clustering. This clustering facilitates a more meaningful grouping of data across domains by aligning similar patterns. During cluster-level domain adaptation, source domain data interact only with semantically similar data in target domain, thereby enhancing the distinguishability of the representations. Extensive experiments on cross-domain node classification tasks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art UGDA approaches, validating its effectiveness in capturing fine-grained similarity.

title: Platform-free proof of federated learning consensus blockchain with optimized neural network-based electronic health records storage and sharing scheme
abstract: The Electronic Health Monitoring System provides the capability to continuously monitor patient health data; however, the current system lacks the capability to protect the patient data from privacy issues, security, and any other type of unauthorized access. To resolve this issue, the current research aims to design the Platform-Free Proof of Federated Learning (PFPoFL) consensus blockchain-based framework that provides a secure and privacy-friendly mechanism to manage electronic health records. In this regard, the proposed work is based on federated learning, which allows hospitals to learn the parameters of the locally trained models on the encrypted datasets without actually exchanging patients’ data. A Hybrid Gorilla Troops Binary Light Spectrum Optimization Algorithm is used for feature selection and a Generative Adversarial Network-based classifier for disease diagnosis, such as pneumonia, heart failure, and tuberculosis. The experimental findings have shown that the proposed framework offers a better outcome in terms of accuracy, security, and scalability. This framework offers higher bandwidth efficiency of 7.2 Mbps than conventional techniques and ensures a stable encryption and decryption process between 78 and 92 s. It is said from the experimental results that the proposed PFPoFL framework offers a secure, scalable, and efficient solution for intelligent healthcare data analysis.

title: A conceptual and logical modeling methodology for data warehousing
abstract: Traditional data warehouse (DW) design approaches often represent measures, granularity hierarchies, and process semantics implicitly, limiting traceability between analytical requirements and logical schema structures. This paper proposes a conceptual and logical modeling methodology (CLMM) that integrates entity–relationship modeling with business–process modeling and treats measures, granularity hierarchies, and process states as explicit conceptual constructs. A formal metamodel, rule-based conceptual-to-logical transformations, and validation constraints are defined to support multi-grain periodic snapshots and process-driven accumulating snapshots. The evaluation covers transformation correctness, semantic error detection, fair query performance comparison, and empirical validation of the process-driven pattern using a real-world event log. The results show that CLMM consistently generates the expected logical structures and detects controlled modeling inconsistencies. Under equivalent schema configurations, CLMM achieves query performance comparable to a manually designed Kimball schema, while improvements over a basic star schema are mainly attributable to multi-granularity pre-aggregation. The results support the methodological feasibility and reproducibility of CLMM, and distributed large-scale scalability remains outside the scope of the present study.

title: Evaluating LLMs for named entity recognition: a cost-benefit analysis in the legal domain
abstract: Abstract Within the legal domain, named entity recognition (NER) is an essential pre-processing tool for important tasks such as information extraction and redaction. Research to date has focused on rule-based approaches or machine learning strategies that require significant time and effort to train through labelled corpora. Large, multi-purpose generative large language models (LLMs) have been successfully employed on natural language processing (NLP) tasks with no prior supervised training and may represent a way forward in addressing these existing bottlenecks. Despite promising results in certain NLP use cases, the Few-Shot LLM performance on unfamiliar, domain-specific NER tasks has, to date, remained uncertain. In this legal clause NER task, we evaluate a Few-Shot, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategy for OpenAI’s GPT-4 LLM on a new CUAD-NER dataset that we have repurposed for the task of Person and Organisation entity identification. In a comparative study, we demonstrate that the GPT4 + Few-Shot CoT prompt strategy outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, achieving a 5% percentage point improvement in Micro F1 score over the best performing BERT base (cased) competitor. This study also takes the novel approach of assessing the business feasibility of deploying each of these machine learning models through a detailed cost–benefit analysis that measures the trade-off between performance metrics and low and high usage running costs.

title: LLM application in digital asset assessments: mixed methods research
abstract: Abstract Digital asset markets are expanding but remain difficult to evaluate, particularly for retail investors who face information overload, unstructured disclosures, and limited regulatory safeguards. Traditional due diligence methods often fail to capture the complexity of blockchain-based projects, exposing investors to misrepresentation and fraud. At the same time, LLMs have shown remarkable results on analyzing large information quantities. Thus, this paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can enhance digital asset assessments by providing inspectable, automated, and low-cost decision support. Using a Design Science Research methodology, we developed a framework and a prototype tool to apply LLM-based evaluation to token-offering whitepapers, evaluated across 1,139 generated runs covering 29 token offerings. We compared different content processing approaches, from raw document analysis to aspect-focused summarization, and tested prompting strategies including Zero-Shot, Few-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought reasoning. Our findings show a nuanced pattern. On aggregate quantitative metrics, structured summarization combined with Chain-of-Thought prompting achieves the lowest rating error, although differences in rank correlation between configurations are not statistically resolvable given the number of projects evaluated; aspect-focused summarization structures criterion-specific evidence and candidate red flags explicitly, but its rating error is higher and the interpretability of this representation was not independently evaluated. To address the single-model limitation, we added a lightweight multi-model robustness check using two small open-source models on a matched subset of cases; the results suggest that the observed optimism bias is not specific to the original closed LLM, although performance still varies across model configurations. Overall agreement between model and expert ratings remains limited, which suggests that LLMs are better understood as decision-support tools for screening and explanation than as substitutes for expert judgment. The study therefore contributes a design-oriented due diligence artifact and a dependence-aware evaluation of how summarization and prompting choices affect calibration, output-level inspectability, and validity boundaries in digital asset assessment.

title: GLCN: a hybrid graph convolution and lite capsule network for robust and interpretable link prediction in complex networks
abstract: Link prediction (LP) algorithms play a critical role in complex networks by inferring potential future connections based on structural patterns and user interaction behavior. However, most existing LP methods struggle to capture hierarchical feature relationships and often fail to model complex part–whole interactions between nodes. These constraints decrease their generalization ability particularly in networks with sparse or noisy connectivity patterns. In order to address these limitations, this paper presents a new hybrid framework, the Graph-Lite Capsule Network (GLCN) that consists of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Lite Capsule Network (LCN). GCN creates node embedding that is regularized by dropout and dimensionality reduction is performed using Principal Component analysis (PCA). These embeddings are processed by LCN, where a Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation is used to better identify meaningful features. After this, the squash function is used to capture meaningful feature relationships, followed by an optimized routing process. At the last stage, the model uses the improved capsule representations to find possible links in the graph. This architecture is very effective in modeling the structural relationships within the graph to ensure greater efficiency. LCN reduces routing steps by eliminating discrete vote matrices and focuses on relevant interactions among the capsules. To understand the efficiency of the proposed method, a comparative evaluation has been performed on six different datasets, each one being a representation of different interaction and collaboration patterns. The findings show that there is an average improvement of about 9.1% in the AUC (Area Under Curve). Additionally, to evaluate the model’s generalization capability, we further compare GLCN with dynamic network-based LP methods, demonstrating its adaptability across evolving graph structures. It also proves its robustness against seven heuristic benchmark methods.

title: KLF: a high-recall learned filter for kNN search
abstract: The K-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) search problem faces significant challenges in high-dimensional spaces due to the curse of dimensionality, which severely degrades the performance of traditional index structures and approximate methods. To address these limitations, we propose KLF (KNN Learned Filter), a neural filtering framework that reformulates kNN search as a dynamic probability-based filtering task. KLF replaces per-query distance computations with neural inference over a pre-trained model, shifting the nature of online computation. KLF employs a multi-layer perceptron to predict the likelihood that each data point is a true k-nearest neighbor to a given query, producing a probability score for every point in the index. A density-aware adaptive threshold then filters these scores to generate compact candidate sets. On the GloVe−200D dataset, KLF achieves 96.6% recall at 1.10 ms; on SIFT1M, it achieves 96.2% recall at 0.90 ms. The candidate sets have a Full Containment Rate of 95.5% with a median size of only 1.2× k , minimizing post-filtering overhead. Rather than claiming universal speed superiority, we position KLF as offering a distinct trade-off: GPU-friendly inference that outputs probability scores for every indexed point—providing a ranking signal that heuristic methods like HNSW, which rely solely on distance metrics, do not offer. We also identify a long-tail performance gap in low-density regions, suggesting directions for future work. These results demonstrate KLF’s effectiveness on million-scale static datasets, with offline training costs amortized over query-intensive workloads.

title: From NER to Business Process Automation: comparative evaluation of CNN, LSTM, and transformer models for address intelligence
abstract: Abstract Named Entity Recognition (NER) can support Business Process Automation (BPA) by converting textual addresses into structured components required for logistics, customer-data management, record validation, and related workflows. Previous studies have commonly evaluated individual neural architectures or single-domain datasets, leaving limited evidence on how heterogeneous model families compare under consistent address-extraction conditions. This study comparatively evaluates five neural architectures—WordCNN, WordLSTM, BERT, DistilBERT, and ELECTRA—for token-level extraction of city, state, country, and postal-code components. Experiments were conducted on two heterogeneous datasets, OASIS aerospace supplier records with 12,059 instances and USA Public Schools records with 102,370 instances, across 50%, 80%, and 100% data-availability regimes. Model-specific tokenization preserved architecture-appropriate input representations, while group-aware holdout partitioning reduced geographic overlap between training and held-out evaluation records. Performance was evaluated using Precision, Recall, F1-score, Accuracy, ROC-AUC, and inference latency. Statistical uncertainty was also reported using 95% confidence intervals for the main accuracy results. At the full-data setting, ELECTRA achieved 99.4% accuracy on OASIS (95% CI: 99.00–99.64%) and 99.6% on USA Public Schools (95% CI: 99.50–99.68%). ELECTRA also required substantially lower measured inference latency than BERT. WordCNN and WordLSTM offered computationally lighter substitutes when faster processing was more important than achieving the highest predictive performance. The main contribution of this study is a controlled comparison of different neural architectures that jointly examines predictive performance, data availability, and computational efficiency for BPA-oriented address extraction.

title: Blockchain-oriented IoHT cybersecurity system utilizing nested dense graph attention capsule networks with circulatory system-based optimization for robust data protection
abstract: The rapid adoption of Internet of Healthcare Things (IoHT) devices has significantly enhanced healthcare services but also exposed systems to cyber threats and data breaches, as medical data is highly sensitive and vulnerable. Current cybersecurity mechanisms often fail to ensure proper integrity, confidentiality, and availability of healthcare data, while noisy datasets and limited computational resources further complicate attack detection and prevention. To address these challenges, this study proposes a blockchain-oriented cybersecurity framework for IoHT, termed Nested Dense Graph Attention Capsule Networks with Circulatory System-Based Optimization for Robust Data Protection (NDGACN-CSBO). The framework leverages data from CICIoMT2024 and WUSTL EHMS 2020 datasets, which are preprocessed using the Adjusted Min–Max with Decimal Scaling and Statistical Column Normalization (AMM-DSSCN) technique to handle inconsistencies and scale features. Feature selection is performed via the Sharpbelly Fish Optimization (SFO) algorithm, ensuring that the most relevant features are retained. Classification of normal and attack patterns is conducted using Nested Dense Graph Attention Capsule Networks (NDGACN), whose performance is further enhanced through Circulatory System-Based Optimization (CSBO) for weight parameter tuning. To secure data sharing, a blockchain-integrated Generation Right Trading (GRT) model with digital smart contracts is employed, enabling tamper-resistant, authenticated, and reliable data exchange in cloud environments. Experimental results demonstrate that NDGACN-CSBO achieves 99.23 and 99.88% accuracy on CICIoMT2024 and WUSTL EHMS 2020 datasets, F1-scores of 99.72 and 99.56%, and ROC values of 99.20 and 99.56%, respectively. The framework ensures strong data privacy and security integrity (> 99%) while efficiently detecting cyber threats, making it highly effective for robust healthcare data protection in IoHT systems.

title: Collaborative enhancement of global and disentangled representations for sequential recommendation
abstract: Users’ interactions with items are driven by complex and diverse intentions. It is an essential task in sequential recommendation to capture users’ real intentions based on historical behavior sequences. Existing methods mostly leverage item-level self-attention mechanism to model item-item transitions, which is susceptible to noises and results in inaccurate attention distribution. In this paper, we propose a novel method called Collaborative Enhancement of Global and Disentangled representations for Sequential Recommendation (CEGDSR). CEGDSR effectively combines global and disentangled intent-aware representations via collaborative enhancement. Specifically, we learn disentangled intent-aware user representations by projecting item representations into multiple intent subspaces. In parallel, we devise attention denoising module to improve global representation. Then, an attention fusion module is designed to fuse intent-level attention information into global attention weights. Finally, we conduct user relationship alignment between enhanced global representation and intent disentangled representation to promote mutual enhancement, which implements better fusion of global and disentangled intent-aware representations. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that CEGDSR outperforms several strong baselines.

title: Quality versus quantity: including imperfect training data improves prediction of user satisfaction in software projects
abstract: This study explored the impact of data quality and quantity on predicting user satisfaction in software projects using the ISBSG dataset. This study evaluated the performance of machine learning models by varying the data variants, i.e. strategies for including low-quality data in the training subsets. A rigorous methodology was employed to ensure the reliability of the results and validate the conclusions. It involved repeated nested cross-validation, standardised accuracy, win–tie–loss analysis, matched-pairs rank biserial correlation, Scott–Knott effect size difference test, and Kendall’s W. The findings suggest that models predicting user satisfaction trained on larger datasets, despite containing low-quality data, usually outperformed those trained on smaller, high-quality datasets. Hence, expanding the training data can improve predictive accuracy, even if it comes at the cost of data quality. Support vector machines (SVM) and extreme gradient boosting trees delivered the most accurate predictions across all data variants. A combination of SVM with the data variant involving all cases and attributes, where at least 40% of values were valid (non-missing), was the most accurate. Obtained findings enabled the formulation of a preliminary recommendation: when working with ISBSG or similar datasets, researchers and practitioners prioritising predictive accuracy of user satisfaction should train models on relatively large datasets, even if they contain some low-quality data, especially when dealing with limited data availability. Provided rankings of data variants, models, and combinations may help set up future studies.

title: A comprehensive review of anomaly detection: from images to videos and compressed video streams
abstract: Anomaly detection (AD) is fundamental element in modern computer vision, allowing intelligent systems to identify abnormalities from typical behavior in images, videos, and compressed video streams. Conventional approaches are limited by statistical or reconstruction-based learning, whereas current advancements in deep and hybrid architectures have revolutionized anomaly detection into a data-driven field capable of modeling intricate spatial–temporal dynamics. This review offers a thorough, interdisciplinary synthesis of 196 formally cited works (161 peer-reviewed journal/conference publications, plus arXiv preprints, doctoral dissertations, and a technical report, included primarily for post-2024 coverage) drawn from a broader corpus of 252 systematically screened papers (2015–2025), presenting a three-stage taxonomy that integrates classical, deep learning, and hybrid or multimodal methodologies. The distinctive contribution of this work is its innovative focus on compressed-domain anomaly detection, a novel approach that utilizes motion vectors, discrete cosine transform coefficients, and residuals directly from encoded streams to enable real-time, privacy-preserving analytics without complete decoding. This study incorporates post-2024 developments such as diffusion-transformer hybrids, federated compressed-learning frameworks, and multimodal vision-language reasoning. It critically assesses the trade-offs between accuracy, latency, scalability, and privacy, highlighting ongoing difficulties in codec generalization and distributed robustness. This review also integrates diverse research across three visual domains, presenting a fresh, codec-agnostic perspective and outlining a roadmap for advanced, efficient, and ethically aligned anomaly detection systems tailored for real-world intelligent multimedia environments.

title: Community-based strategies for user-driven competitive influence maximization in social networks
abstract: Abstract Nowadays, people in the modern world communicate with their friends, relatives, and colleagues through the internet. Persons/nodes and communication/edges among them form a network. Social media networks are a type of network where people share their views with the community. There are several models that cap- ture human behavior, such as a reaction to the information received from friends or relatives. The two fundamental models of information diffusion widely dis- cussed in the social networks are the Independent Cascade Model and the Linear Threshold Model. Liu et al. [1] propose a variant of the linear threshold model in their paper title User-driven competitive influence Maximization(UDCIM) in social networks. Authors try to simulate human behavior where they do not make a decision immediately after being influenced, but take a pause for a while, and then they make a final decision. They propose the heuristic algorithms and prove the approximation factor under community constraints( The seed vertices belong to an identical community). Even finding the community is itself an NP- hard problem. In this article, we extend the existing work with algorithms and LP-formation of the problem. We also implement and test the LP-formulated equations on small datasets by using the Gurobi Solver [2]. We furthermore pro- pose one heuristic and one genetic algorithm. The extensive experimentation is carried out on medium to large datasets, and the outcomes of both algorithms are plotted in the results and discussion section

title: Biomedical word sense disambiguation based on capsule gated recurrent unit
abstract: Words in field of biomedicine usually have ambiguity, so it is very important to understand their meanings correctly for both medical research and clinical practice. In this paper, we propose a method for word sense disambiguation (WSD) of biomedical vocabulary based on capsule gated recurrent unit (GRU). It combines semantic compression ability of capsule neural network with context modeling ability of gated recurrent unit, which can accurately disambiguate polysemous words in biomedical texts. Disambiguation features include word, part of speech, and meanings. Bert is used to vectorize features, GRU is applied to enhance the network’s ability to understand and remember sequences, capsule neural network is adopted to extract spatial hierarchical structure, and linear transformation is used to compute probability distribution of biomedical ambiguous word under each semantic category in classification layer. Semantic category with the highest probability is determined as category of biomedical ambiguous word. We use MSH dataset to optimize the proposed network and testify it. Experimental results show that the proposed method can significantly improve average accuracy of biomedical WSD.

title: Unifying global and local anomaly detection for time series
abstract: Abstract Anomaly detection for time series data has been proven useful from both academia and industry, and can be categorized into global and local methodsbased on the range of data used to determine anomalies. To the best of our knowledge, there are no methods that unify the global and local methods together.In this study, we propose an approach that unifies the global and local anomaly detection to achieve the good performance. To make the unification possible, wediscretize time series data and partition the discrete data into global and local anomaly detection parts based on a concept of local factor. We design a rule-based global method using non-redundant association rules with tolerances to handle the difficulty of the latency phenomenon and the excessive number ofrules in time series data. We develop a Transformer based on local method with LSH (Locality Sensitive Hashing) Attention to fit better for discrete data. Wefinally conduct an extensive experimental study to verify the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach.

title: A Jensen–Shannon divergence-based item similarity method for multi-criteria collaborative filtering
abstract: Multi-criteria collaborative filtering enables users to evaluate items across multiple dimensions, leading to more refined recommendations. However, traditional methods, including multidimensional distance-based approaches, rely heavily on common ratings between users or items. In sparse data scenarios, this reliance often results in reduced accuracy due to limited overlapping ratings. Despite improvements in similarity calculations, many existing approaches continue to struggle with data sparsity and fail to capture complex item relationships. To address this challenge, a novel item-based similarity method is introduced, utilizing Jensen–Shannon divergence within a multi-criteria collaborative filtering framework. By computing item similarities based on probability density values rather than common ratings, the approach demonstrates enhanced effectiveness in sparse datasets where traditional correlation-based techniques are limited. When overlapping users are available, their count is incorporated as a weighting factor to further refine similarity calculations. Experimental results show that the proposed methods achieve lower prediction error than existing methods in most evaluated configurations, particularly under sparse conditions, with the advantage narrowing as dataset density increases. Statistical significance analysis indicates the robustness of these improvements across different experimental configurations, while runtime evaluation demonstrates computational efficiency comparable to existing sparsity-aware methods. These outcomes confirm that the proposed methods substantially improve recommendation accuracy in sparse data environments.

title: TransDualKGR: a transformer-based dynamic representation and dual-agent framework for multi-hop reasoning over knowledge graphs
abstract: To tackle the challenges posed by the rigidity of static representations, the coupled nature of the action space, and the oversimplified reward mechanisms in multi-hop knowledge graph reasoning, we introduce the TransDualKGR framework. We combine a Transformer-enhanced dynamic representation module with a dual-agent (relation and entity) architecture to enable collaborative reasoning. Specifically, the Transformer module employs a relation-conditioned attention mechanism and Graph Positional Encoding (GraphPE) to capture topological structures. Meanwhile, we adopt PageRank-based neighbor sampling to generate dynamic context-aware entity embeddings. Moreover, we innovatively devise a hierarchically decoupled dual-agent architecture. The relation agent is designed to optimize the search within the relation space, effectively compressing the action space to |R| dimensions. On the other hand, the entity agent locates the target entity based on the selected relation, restricting the action space to the subset of entities connected by that relation. These two agents collaborate through a shared LSTM state. We also propose a quadruple dynamic reward function to jointly optimize four aspects: the destination reward, the path efficiency reward, the PageRank-guided entity influence factor reward, and the diversity reward driven by dynamic embedding variance. Extensive experiments conducted on FB15k-237, WN18RR, and NELL-995 demonstrate that our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines on most metrics. It improves the Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) by 6.0%, 2.4%, and 4.4% on these datasets, respectively. Additionally, on FB15k-237 the path diversity index reaches 0.43 at T = 3.

title: Fuzzy quantum-driven sentiment-aware recommendation system using Hamiltonian quantum generative self-attention Dandelion network
abstract: With the rapid expansion of the online business, vast amounts of diverse customer data have been generated, making it difficult to leverage customer preferences efficiently, perform sentiment analysis from product reviews, and accurately recommend products. The accuracy of current recommendation systems is decreased due to issues with cold start, data sparsity, and the complexity of the linguistic expressions in customer evaluations. The research introduced the method named Hamiltonian quantum generative self-attention dandelion network (HQGSD-Net), an integrated approach that incorporates five different datasets for comprehensive sentiment and behavioral analysis. The data are pre-processed by using quality-driven fuzzy min–max neural networks (QDFMM Net) with tokenization, POS tagging, and parsing to clean the review comments by eliminating stop words, recognizing adjectives, and establishing semantic links. The fuzzy rule-based adaptive kernel-regularized fuzzy C-means clustering algorithm (AKRFCCA) is used to identify customer sentiments and product similarities in order to extract features and generate recommendations. In order to increase efficiency and improve forecasts for sentiment scores that could be either positive, negative, or neutral, the HQGSD-Net model combines Hamiltonian quantum generative adversarial networks (HQuGANs) with single-head self-attention (SHSA) and DOA. The dandelion optimizer algorithm (DOA) is used for the optimization process. It has been seen from the experiment that the proposed system provides accurate results in recommending customers' interests at a 99.9% accuracy level. Beyond improving sentiment-based personalization, this approach is flexible for different product categories and scalable to real-life e-commerce data.

title: Feature selection strategies for improving MinHash-based classifiers’ performance and generalization
abstract: MinHash is a sketching algorithm widely employed for estimating similarity in large-scale datasets, generating independent hash-based features that serve as unbiased estimators of the Jaccard similarity. While these properties offer advantages in terms of storage efficiency and computational cost, they also render many conventional feature selection (FS) methods ineffective. This paper presents the first systematic exploration of FS strategies tailored to MinHash-based classifiers. We propose four FS methods: statistical, inter-class dissimilarity, intra-class similarity, and a hybrid approach, explicitly designed to exploit the nominal and independent nature of MinHash. We also introduce a novel feature aggregation strategy combining MinHash outputs from multiple sketches to enhance classifier performance. While applying FS methods to MinHash-based datasets does not preserve the Jaccard similarity, in our case, rather than maintaining exact similarity properties, our sole objective is to improve machine-learning classifier performance through an intelligent selection of the most beneficial MinHash-based features, a relatively underexplored research direction in the existing literature. We perform evaluations on five diverse real-world tasks: (1) unknown malware detection in Linux volatile memory, (2) COVID-19 diagnosis from chest X-rays, (3) virus DNA categorization, (4) fake news detection, and (5) malicious PDF identification. The evaluation shows that our methods generally outperform widely used FS techniques for nominal data, with statistically significant improvements observed in the majority of experimental settings. These improvements are associated with improved generalization performance, reduced model complexity, and lower storage requirements. However, performance gains are not uniform across all datasets and configurations, indicating sensitivity to dataset characteristics and classifier choice. Our objective is to enhance the performance of MinHash-based classifiers for a given MinHash dataset, rather than to identify the optimal classifier for a given learning task. In other words, our focus lies in improving the applicability and effectiveness of existing learning algorithms when they leverage MinHash-derived features, rather than in pursuing the theoretical upper bound of classification performance. The experimental results show that our methods improve classifiers’ generalization capabilities under the MinHash hyperparameter settings evaluated across five domains, and that similar improvements are observed under the alternative sketch configurations tested in Experiment 2.

title: Two-stage augmentation and dual-expert modeling for robust sentiment analysis on imbalanced texts
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for sentiment analysis on imbalanced datasets, leveraging a dual-expert architecture and two-stage data augmentation for enhanced performance. We first address the challenge of limited minority class representation in the highly imbalanced Twitter US-Airline Sentiment dataset (approximately 63% negative, 21% neutral, and 16% positive) by applying data augmentation through paraphrasing and back-translation using Italian as an intermediary language. In the second stage, we augment the original text by enveloping key emotional aspects with special tokens [start aspect] and [end aspect] to improve model comprehension. Our approach tackles the overlooked challenge of short, nuanced social media texts—laden with sarcasm, emojis, and context-dependent meanings—where traditional methods often fail due to overfitting and high computational demands. The augmented data are processed through a pipeline utilizing a T5 text-to-text generative model as Expert 1 for unsupervised key emotional aspect extraction, followed by a RoBERTa-base model as Expert 2 for sentiment extraction, and a SoftMax layer for classification. We fine-tune the models under a rigorous experimental setup, employing cross-validation with k=fivefold and k=tenfold. Experiments on three datasets—Yelp, Twitter US-Airline Sentiment, and StanfordNLP/IMDB Review—demonstrate the framework’s efficacy. Using k=10 over 2 epochs, our model achieves 98.5% accuracy, 98.5% precision, 98.5% recall, and an F1-score of 98.5% on the Twitter dataset, significantly outperforming the baseline model which plateaued at 92% for both accuracy and F1-score. This highlights the effectiveness of two-stage data augmentation, specialized tokenization, and a dual-expert approach in robust sentiment analysis for imbalanced datasets.

title: Navigating scalability to enhance service discovery and recommendations with graph-based embedding models
abstract: Semantic web service discovery faces scalability challenges associated with increasing repository size, heterogeneous ontology structures, and the computational overhead of semantic matching and ranking. This work presents a clustering-assisted knowledge graph embedding (KGE) framework for semantic web service discovery and recommendation. An integrated knowledge graph semantic web service (KGSWS) repository was constructed from 48 OWLS-TC v4 ontologies containing 1083 semantic web services. In Phase 1, TransE, ComplEx, and DistMult were optimized over KGSWS to learn semantic representations through link prediction evaluation. Among the evaluated models, TransE achieved the best embedding quality with MRR of 0.5792 and Hits@10 value of 0.6716. In Phase 2, the learned representations were evaluated using different clustering techniques to support candidate search-space reduction prior to service ranking. In Phase 3, recommendation performance was evaluated using 38 benchmark queries in terms of Precision@10, Recall@10, NDCG@10, and MAP@10. The TransE + K-Means configuration obtained average values of 0.9579, 0.7207, 0.9667, and 0.9873, respectively. Differences among the evaluated configurations were further examined using the Friedman test followed by Dunn–Bonferroni post hoc analysis. For the evaluated repository settings, the scalability analysis obtained a search-space reduction of 82.73%, a query-processing speedup of 3.61×, and a latency reduction of 72.27% for the complete repository. The memory analysis indicated a 54.66% reduction in storage for the embedding representation relative to the serialized ontology representation under the adopted storage calculation. Quantitative comparison against ontology-based semantic matching showed improvements of 13.75% in Precision@10, 19.84% in Recall@10, 11.80% in NDCG@10, and 18.72% in MAP@10. Therefore, the evaluated results indicate that combining KGE-based semantic representations with clustering-assisted candidate selection can reduce the service search space while maintaining retrieval and ranking performance under the benchmark and experimental settings considered in this study.
